paragraphs: Adjoint Sampling learns diffusion processes for drawing samples from an energy function or an unnormalized probability density. Its central computational contribution is to permit many more gradient updates than energy evaluations and model samples. This matters because learning progress can continue without requiring an equally large increase in those sampling and evaluation operations.

The method is an on-policy approach grounded in stochastic optimal control. It inherits the theoretical guarantees of Adjoint Matching and can train without additional corrective procedures that move samples toward the desired distribution. The framework also incorporates symmetries and periodic boundaries, supporting molecular descriptions based on either Cartesian positions or torsional coordinates.

The experiments cover classical energy functions and larger energy models represented by neural networks. For the latter, the authors demonstrate amortized conformer generation across multiple molecular systems: a learned sampling approach supports generating molecular configurations across many systems. Together, these results support the method’s stated scalability and its relevance to computational chemistry.
icml-2025-adjoint-sampling-highly-scalab.tldr: Adjoint Sampling scales diffusion-based energy sampling by enabling many training updates per energy evaluation or model sample.

paragraphs: This paper examines a tension between recognizing unfamiliar inputs and generalizing successfully to them. The authors empirically connect both objectives to the degree of neural collapse in a network layer. Stronger collapse improves out-of-distribution detection in their study, but weakens generalization; reducing collapse reverses that pattern. Their findings suggest that asking one feature space to serve both objectives creates a trade-off.

The authors develop a theoretical framework relating neural collapse to these two outcomes. They identify two ways to influence it: entropy regularization reduces collapse to support generalization, while a fixed Simplex ETF projector promotes collapse to support detection. These mechanisms give the model explicit controls over a property associated with competing objectives.

The resulting method controls neural collapse at different network layers, allowing different representations to support different needs. Experiments across out-of-distribution datasets and network architectures show strong performance on both tasks. The contribution is therefore a layer-specific approach to managing the observed tension, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation.
icml-2025-controlling-neural-collapse-en.tldr: Controlling neural collapse at different network layers helps reconcile unfamiliar-input detection with generalization.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller language model using knowledge from a larger teacher, but the training itself can remain expensive. DA-KD targets a source of that expense: existing methods overlook differences in sample difficulty and spend effort distilling easy examples unnecessarily. Its framework dynamically changes the distillation dataset according to how difficult its samples are.

Focusing on difficult examples creates another problem. The authors observe that existing distillation losses can become ineffective when difficult samples dominate the dataset, because optimization becomes unstable and hard examples are neglected. They introduce bidirectional discrepancy loss to address this issue alongside the dataset adjustment. The approach therefore changes both which examples receive attention and how the student learns from them.

Experiments report that DA-KD can exceed existing state-of-the-art distillation methods by 2% while using half the training cost. The authors also report a case where the student surpasses its teacher with 4.7-fold compression. These findings support the value of coordinating difficulty-aware data selection with a loss suited to the resulting training set.
icml-2025-da-kd-difficulty-aware-knowled.tldr: DA-KD combines difficulty-aware sample selection with a new distillation loss to train smaller language models more efficiently.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models generate data through repeated sampling steps, which makes generation slow. Speeding them up requires handling relationships among discrete elements, such as image pixels or positions in a language sequence. Modeling those relationships directly through a high-dimensional joint distribution is computationally costly, creating a challenge for reducing the number of steps.

The paper proposes scalable mixture models that capture correlations across dimensions, together with loss functions for distilling existing diffusion models. Its theoretical analysis explains why conventional models that treat elements independently can still approximate the data distribution well, but essentially need many sampling steps. The proposed losses let mixture models learn the correlations needed to compress that longer process into a few steps.

Experiments demonstrate the approach on pretrained discrete diffusion models for both images and language. The findings connect faster sampling to the model’s ability to represent dependencies between elements. Learning these dependencies gives the distilled model a way to carry out in fewer iterations what the conventional model achieves through a longer sequence.
icml-2025-distillation-of-discrete-diffu.tldr: Scalable mixture models learn correlations between discrete elements to distill many-step diffusion models into few-step generators.

paragraphs: Double-Filter makes adapting pretrained vision-language models more efficient by reducing redundancy in two places: the image features presented to the model and the layers used to process them. This treats fine-tuning cost as a combined input and architecture problem, with both parts contributing opportunities to reduce unnecessary computation while retaining useful representations.

For the input side, the method separates background and foreground before applying a refined image-patch selection procedure. This is intended to preserve more comprehensive semantic information while improving inference efficiency. For the architecture side, a genetic algorithm searches for redundant components at a fine-grained layer level. Removing these components reduces architectural redundancy while limiting the impact on model performance.

The authors evaluate Double-Filter on visual question answering, natural-language visual reasoning, and retrieval, using the METER and ViLT model families. They report better fine-tuning efficiency and competitive task performance compared with advanced efficient fine-tuning methods. The findings support combining selective visual inputs with selective model structure as a practical approach to efficient adaptation.
icml-2025-double-filter-efficient-fine-t.tldr: Double-Filter reduces vision-language adaptation costs by filtering redundant image patches and model layers.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects becomes complicated when individuals interact through a market or recommendation system. A change affecting one person can alter conditions that others also experience. This paper formalizes such connections as shared-state interference, with prices, algorithmic recommendations, and social signals serving as examples of states through which individuals are linked.

The central modeling assumption is that individuals’ potential outcomes are independent once the shared state is taken into account. This allows dependence through a common state while placing a specific restriction on what dependence remains after conditioning on it. Under that structure, the authors extend a double machine learning theorem and establish conditions that allow efficient statistical inference.

They then apply the general result to several models in which the average direct effect or global average treatment effect can be estimated efficiently. The contribution is a framework connecting a recognizable form of interaction to formal inference guarantees. Those guarantees are conditional on the shared-state formulation and the theorem’s requirements, rather than covering arbitrary forms of interference.
icml-2025-double-machine-learning-for-ca.tldr: The paper extends double machine learning to treatment-effect estimation when interactions operate through shared states under a conditional-independence assumption.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer a brain-inspired approach to energy-efficient computation, but learning methods face a difficult trade-off. Direct spatial-temporal backpropagation carries substantial training overhead, while converting an artificial neural network into a spiking network can create high inference latency. This paper combines conversion with parallel spiking computation to address these obstacles.

The proposed framework mathematically links each time step of parallel spiking neurons to the cumulative spike firing rate. The authors establish lossless and sorting properties for the conversion process and identify an optimal shifting distance at each step. These results give the conversion procedure a theoretical basis for coordinating spiking calculations across time steps.

The framework also incorporates distribution-aware error calibration, enabling efficient conversion for more general activation functions or settings without additional training. Experiments across conversion cases report substantial performance advantages at extremely low temporal latency. The contribution is the joint use of parallel spiking calculation and network conversion, with theoretical properties and empirical results supporting its promise for supervised spiking-network learning.
icml-2025-faster-and-stronger-when-ann-s.tldr: Combining network conversion with parallel spiking computation enables effective spiking neural networks at very low temporal latency.

paragraphs: Predictive models often reveal their weaknesses only after deployment, leading to repeated cycles of collecting difficult examples and retraining. This paper proposes discovering such weaknesses proactively by generating additional training examples. Its Longtail Guidance method steers a latent diffusion model toward inputs that signals from the predictive model identify as rare or difficult.

The authors develop general signals for this purpose, including a differentiable measure of epistemic uncertainty computed in one forward pass. They state that this formulation leaves model parameters and predictive performance unaffected. The guidance process requires no retraining of either the diffusion model or predictive model, and the predictor does not need to process intermediate diffusion states.

Generated examples show meaningful semantic variation and produce significant generalization improvements across multiple image-classification benchmarks. A vision-language model can also analyze them to explain conceptual gaps in words. This connects data generation with diagnosis: the same process can supply useful training examples and help reveal which concepts a deployed predictor handles poorly.
icml-2025-generative-data-mining-with-lo.tldr: Longtail Guidance steers diffusion generation toward a predictor’s difficult cases to improve generalization and expose conceptual gaps.

paragraphs: GIVE addresses reasoning tasks where a language model’s internal knowledge is insufficient and a comprehensive external knowledge base may be expensive or unavailable. It combines information stored in model parameters with external knowledge, aiming to improve reasoning while requiring only limited outside input. The method works without additional model training.

Its reasoning process has three stages. The agent first selects relevant expert information, then develops associations specific to the query, and finally combines that information into an answer. This observe-reflect-speak structure organizes how internal and external knowledge contribute to the result. The authors describe the resulting reasoning process as fully interpretable.

Experiments report improvements across model sizes and both scientific and open-domain assessments. In some scientific settings, a smaller model using GIVE exceeds a larger model’s performance. Reported accuracy improvements reach from 43.5% to 88.2%, and evaluated knowledge graphs range from 135 to more than 840,000 nodes. These findings support the method’s usefulness with both small restricted sources and large noisy ones.
icml-2025-give-structured-reasoning-of-l.tldr: GIVE structures training-free language-model reasoning around selecting, reflecting on, and synthesizing internal and external knowledge.

paragraphs: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning seeks one policy that can solve several tasks using previously collected experience. Because the learner cannot interact with the environment during learning, it must extract useful structure from a dataset mixing different tasks. GO-Skill addresses the difficulty of sharing knowledge across those tasks by organizing experience into reusable skills.

The method first extracts skills through a goal-oriented process and uses vector quantization to build a discrete skill library. A skill enhancement stage then addresses imbalances between skills that apply broadly and skills specific to particular tasks. This refinement targets a tension in shared learning: widely useful behavior and specialized behavior both need adequate representation.

Finally, hierarchical policy learning builds a higher-level policy that selects and coordinates the discrete skills for a requested task. Experiments on varied robotic manipulation tasks in MetaWorld demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and versatility. The results support reusable skill abstraction as a way to transfer knowledge within offline multi-task learning while preserving the ability to handle distinct task requirements.
icml-2025-goal-oriented-skill-abstractio.tldr: GO-Skill turns mixed offline experience into a reusable discrete skill library coordinated by a higher-level policy.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can learn from information about individuals, making privacy protection important when node features contain sensitive data. Existing approaches using local differential privacy can substantially distort the graph data and reduce learning quality, including node-classification accuracy. UPGNET aims to preserve useful learning while protecting the information supplied by users.

The framework introduces a three-stage pipeline that generalizes local differential privacy protocols for node features. Its analysis identifies feature dimension and neighborhood size as two key influences on learning utility. These findings connect the privacy problem to how much information each node represents and the neighborhood structure through which graph learning operates.

UPGNET responds with a High-Order Aggregator layer and a Node Feature Regularization layer, making these two concerns part of the learning architecture. Experiments on real-world datasets report significant improvements over existing methods in both privacy protection and learning utility. The paper’s contribution combines analysis of what drives utility loss with architectural components designed to improve learning under the privacy framework.
icml-2025-going-deeper-into-locally-diff.tldr: UPGNET improves private graph learning by addressing the effects of feature dimension and neighborhood size on utility.

paragraphs: Models deployed over time encounter changing data distributions. Methods for evolving domain generalization try to learn these changes, but may pick up shortcuts linking task-irrelevant factors to prediction targets. This paper proposes SYNC, which uses a causal account of temporal change to learn representations intended to generalize as domains evolve.

The authors design a time-aware structural causal model that includes both changing causal factors and shifts in causal mechanisms. SYNC implements this perspective through a sequential variational autoencoder with specially designed information-theoretic objectives. It also preserves compact representations of causal factors belonging to the same class, both within a domain and across domains.

The theoretical analysis shows that the method can yield an optimal causal predictor for each time domain. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior temporal generalization. Together, these findings support modeling how causal information evolves, alongside keeping same-class causal representations coherent, as a way to reduce the influence of misleading temporal correlations on prediction.
icml-2025-learning-time-aware-causal-rep.tldr: SYNC learns time-aware causal representations to improve generalization as data distributions and causal mechanisms evolve.

paragraphs: A quiver is a directed multigraph, and mutation is an operation that transforms one quiver into another. In cluster algebra, a central question asks whether two quivers can be connected by a sequence of mutations. This paper uses graph neural networks to investigate that equivalence problem and find mathematical structure across collections of examples.

The authors combine graph learning with explainability techniques to independently discover mutation-equivalence criteria for quivers of type tilde D. The role of explainability is central to the contribution: the investigation seeks identifiable mathematical criteria, extending the use of the model beyond producing a prediction about the examples it encounters.

The learned hidden representations also contain structure that allows the researchers to reconstruct known criteria for type D, even though the model was not explicitly trained to capture those criteria. This finding provides evidence that learned representations can encode abstract mathematical rules. Within the studied quiver families, the work illustrates how graph models and interpretation methods can support mathematical discovery.
icml-2025-machines-and-mathematical-muta.tldr: Graph neural networks and explainability methods uncover quiver mutation-equivalence criteria and recover mathematical structure in hidden representations.

paragraphs: Olica compresses large language models through structured pruning without retraining. It addresses the cost of repairing relationships disrupted when model components are removed. Its attention-layer approach starts from the observation that computation depends on products linking query with key matrices and value with output matrices, making those paired relationships central to compression.

The method treats each matrix product as a whole and applies principal component analysis to preserve its most important information. The authors describe this as preserving accuracy and the original structure while removing the need for retraining. A faster decomposition reduces PCA complexity by a factor equal to the square of the attention-head count.

For feed-forward layers, Olica addresses accumulated pruning errors with linear calibration. Two low-rank matrices reconstruct residual errors, obtained through singular value decomposition of a least-squares solution. This repair also avoids retraining. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report superior performance alongside efficient data usage, GPU memory consumption, and runtime, supporting the combination of relationship-aware compression and direct error calibration.
icml-2025-olica-efficient-structured-pru.tldr: Olica prunes language models without retraining by compressing attention matrix products and directly calibrating feed-forward errors.

paragraphs: Pruning simplifies decision trees, helping make models more efficient and interpretable. This paper asks how difficult it is to find an optimal pruning when using two operations common in heuristics: subtree replacement and subtree raising. The authors analyze both classical computational complexity and how difficulty changes with particular properties of the input.

The two operations have sharply different complexity. Optimal subtree replacement is solvable in polynomial time, whereas optimal subtree raising is NP-complete. For raising, the analysis identifies parameter choices and combinations that allow fixed-parameter tractability, as well as choices that leave the problem hard. This gives a more detailed picture than a single worst-case classification.

For example, keeping only the feature-domain size D or only the number of features d small does not remove the stated hardness. Considering them together yields a running time of D^(2d) times a polynomial in input size. Preliminary experiments complement the theory, illustrating its practical implications for choosing pruning procedures and identifying settings where optimal simplification is computationally approachable.
icml-2025-optimal-decision-tree-pruning-.tldr: Optimal decision-tree pruning is polynomial-time for subtree replacement but NP-complete for subtree raising, with tractability depending on combined input parameters.

paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks learn to sample objects with probabilities proportional to their rewards, allowing them to discover varied high-quality solutions. Although they resemble reinforcement learning through sequential decision-making, connections to ordinary reinforcement learning have received less attention than connections to entropy-regularized methods. This paper investigates a link through policy evaluation.

The authors find that the value function obtained by evaluating a uniform policy is closely related to GFlowNet flow functions. They use that relationship to construct rectified random policy evaluation, or RPE. The algorithm obtains the reward-matching behavior associated with GFlowNets by evaluating a fixed random policy, offering a different route to the same sampling objective.

Across extensive benchmarks, RPE achieves results competitive with previous approaches. The significance is conceptual as well as algorithmic: a basic reinforcement-learning operation can support the diverse, reward-proportional sampling sought by GFlowNets. This connection offers a way to express that capability through established reinforcement-learning ideas and broadens the role of policy evaluation beyond its usual use in reward-maximizing learning.
icml-2025-random-policy-evaluation-uncov.tldr: Rectified random policy evaluation connects ordinary reinforcement learning to the reward-proportional sampling behavior of GFlowNets.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a task in which natural-language descriptions identify objects to segment inside a 3D Gaussian scene. Descriptions can depend on object attributes or spatial relationships. The challenge includes identifying an object that is occluded or not directly visible from a new viewpoint, requiring understanding that goes beyond what is immediately visible.

The authors create Ref-LERF, the first dataset for this referring-segmentation task. Their analysis identifies understanding across language and 3D information, together with modeling spatial relationships, as central difficulties. They then introduce ReferSplat, which explicitly connects 3D Gaussian points with language expressions through a spatially aware framework.

ReferSplat achieves state-of-the-art performance on the new task and on 3D open-vocabulary segmentation benchmarks. The contribution combines a task definition, a dataset, and a method for grounding language in a spatial scene representation. Its results support the importance of explicit 3D and language modeling for selecting described objects, a capability the authors identify as relevant to advancing embodied AI.
icml-2025-refersplat-referring-segmentat.tldr: ReferSplat grounds natural-language object descriptions in 3D Gaussian scenes using explicit spatial modeling.

paragraphs: SafeMap addresses high-definition map construction for autonomous driving when some camera views are unavailable. Missing views leave the system with an incomplete account of its surroundings, which existing methods can struggle to handle. The framework combines reconstruction of perspective-view information with correction of the bird’s-eye-view representation used for mapping.

Its Gaussian-based Perspective View Reconstruction module uses prior knowledge about view importance and relationships between the available cameras. It dynamically prioritizes regions that are most informative. The Distillation-based Bird’s-Eye-View Correction module then uses panoramic bird’s-eye-view features to improve representations built from incomplete observations. The two components address missing information at complementary stages of the mapping process.

The authors present SafeMap as a plug-and-play framework that is straightforward to incorporate into existing systems. Experiments report significant improvements over previous methods when camera observations are complete and when some are missing. These results support the value of combining selective reconstruction with representation correction to improve mapping robustness, rather than treating missing-camera cases as a separate mapping task.
icml-2025-safemap-robust-hd-map-construc.tldr: SafeMap combines perspective reconstruction and bird’s-eye-view correction to improve HD mapping when camera views are missing.

paragraphs: Off-dynamics reinforcement learning studies agents trained under transition dynamics that differ from those encountered at deployment. This paper considers robust learning when an agent can gather experience only by interacting online with the training environment. That restriction makes exploration central: the learner cannot freely query arbitrary state-action pairs or rely on a dataset already covering deployment states.

The authors introduce the supremal visitation ratio to quantify mismatch between training and deployment dynamics. They show that an unbounded ratio makes online learning exponentially hard. This identifies a concrete source of difficulty arising from the relationship between the environment available for exploration and the environments against which robustness is required.

For transition uncertainty described using f-divergences, the paper proposes a computationally efficient algorithm with sublinear regret. Matching lower bounds establish optimal dependence on both the visitation ratio and the number of interaction episodes. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution links exploration difficulty to a measurable mismatch quantity and characterizes achievable learning performance in this online setting.
icml-2025-sample-complexity-of-distribut.tldr: The paper quantifies exploration difficulty under changing dynamics and gives an efficient robust-learning algorithm with matching regret bounds on key factors.

paragraphs: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning adds new categories over time without retaining examples from earlier ones. The paper focuses on two causes of forgetting: old classes move within the model’s embedding space, and the classifier becomes biased toward new classes because training uses only new data. DPCR addresses these representation and decision problems together.

To estimate movement in the embedding space, DPCR combines a learnable transformation with a row-space projection. This dual-projection approach captures shifts affecting whole tasks and shifts affecting individual categories. The estimated changes then calibrate class prototypes and covariance information used in rebuilding the classifier, connecting representation adjustment directly to the classification step.

The reconstruction uses a ridge-regression formulation to reduce bias toward recently learned tasks. Experiments across multiple datasets report a better balance between old and new tasks and stronger performance than state-of-the-art exemplar-free methods. The findings support correcting both where earlier classes are represented and how the classifier uses those representations when the original examples are no longer retained.
icml-2025-semantic-shift-estimation-via-.tldr: DPCR estimates representation shifts and reconstructs the classifier to reduce forgetting without retaining old examples.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train collaboratively, but malicious participants can implant backdoors that affect targeted inputs. Defenses based on isolated client behavior and fixed rules can be bypassed by adaptive attackers. SPMC instead uses consistency across collaborating clients to estimate their marginal contributions and determine how strongly their updates should influence learning.

Its collaboration mechanism dynamically reduces the influence of clients whose behavior departs from the collaborative norm. The authors present this as a way to remain robust when the number of attackers changes. A second, local self-purification mechanism adjusts suspicious gradients by aligning them with margin-based model updates, reducing the effect of poisoning within clients.

Together, the two mechanisms address defense at both server and client levels and tackle weaknesses associated with proxy-dependent purification. Experiments on several classification benchmarks show strong protection against sophisticated backdoor attacks while preserving accuracy on benign tasks. The reported results support combining adaptive contribution assessment with local gradient correction to strengthen federated learning against the evaluated attacks.
icml-2025-spmc-self-purifying-federated-.tldr: SPMC defends federated learning by reducing anomalous clients’ influence and locally correcting suspicious gradients.

paragraphs: Subspace optimization methods reduce memory requirements when training or fine-tuning large language models, but their behavior under stochastic gradients needs theoretical justification. This paper examines GaLore and constructs an explicit counterexample showing that it does not always converge to an optimal solution. Memory efficiency alone therefore does not establish reliable convergence.

The authors identify sufficient conditions under which GaLore does converge: using a sufficiently large mini-batch or having isotropic gradient noise. These are alternative conditions, not claims that either is necessary in every convergent case. The analysis clarifies how the stochastic setting affects the method and gives concrete circumstances in which convergence can be established.

The paper then introduces GoLore, a variant based on random low-rank gradient projection. It provably converges in typical stochastic settings even with standard batch sizes. The authors also extend their analysis to other subspace optimization algorithms and empirically validate the theoretical results. The contribution pairs a diagnosis of GaLore’s possible failure with a modified approach carrying broader stochastic convergence guarantees.
icml-2025-subspace-optimization-for-larg.tldr: GoLore uses random low-rank gradient projection to provide stochastic convergence guarantees after identifying cases where GaLore fails.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning adapts a foundation model to a specialized domain, but can erode knowledge acquired during pretraining. This paper finds that combining a pretrained language model with its fine-tuned counterpart helps preserve general knowledge. More strikingly, the combination can outperform the fine-tuned model on its own specialized domain, revealing what the authors call overadaptation.

The theoretical explanation centers on balancing two errors. Too little fine-tuning leaves bias because adaptation is insufficient; overfitting the fine-tuning data introduces variance. Ensembling balances these effects, and the authors show it can address the trade-off more effectively than regularization in their analysis. This explains why preserving some pretrained influence can benefit even the adaptation task.

The formal results concern over-parameterized linear settings, where interpolating between pretrained and fine-tuned weights significantly improves performance. Empirical experiments are consistent with that account. The findings provide theoretical support for the observed ensemble benefits while locating the formal analysis in a specific model setting, connecting the practical phenomenon to an explicit bias-variance explanation.
icml-2025-understanding-overadaptation-i.tldr: Combining pretrained and fine-tuned models can counter overadaptation and improve performance even on the fine-tuning domain.

paragraphs: Ordinary generative modeling transports samples from a source distribution toward a target distribution. In some applications, however, each object being generated is itself a distribution, such as a point cloud describing a shape. Wasserstein flow matching extends flow matching to families of these objects, using Wasserstein geometry to respect their distributional structure.

The theoretical contribution establishes that Wasserstein geodesics provide valid conditional flows over the space of distributions. This supplies a foundation for the training objective. The algorithm combines optimal transport with attention and handles two representations: Gaussian distributions, for which it uses closed-form transport paths, and general distributions represented by point clouds, for which it uses entropic estimates.

The method generates two- and three-dimensional shapes as well as high-dimensional cellular microenvironments from spatial transcriptomics data. These demonstrations show its reach across different representations and dimensionalities. The key contribution is making distributions themselves the units of generation, with a flow construction that incorporates their geometry instead of treating their internal structure as incidental.
icml-2025-wasserstein-flow-matching-gene.tldr: Wasserstein flow matching generates whole distributions by extending flow matching to their optimal-transport geometry.

paragraphs: Autoregressive image generation repeatedly predicts visual tokens, making the number of model forward passes a major source of generation cost. ZipAR accelerates this process without retraining. Its starting observation is that images have local structure and widely separated regions tend to depend only weakly on one another, creating opportunities to decode tokens in parallel.

Given tokens already decoded, ZipAR retains next-token prediction along the row dimension while also decoding tokens in adjacent column regions in parallel. An adaptive local-window assignment determines the context used for each token. Rejection sampling, analogous to that used in speculative decoding, helps align parallel predictions with each token’s contextual requirements.

This allows one forward pass to produce multiple tokens and reduces the passes needed to complete an image. Experiments on Emu3-Gen report reductions of up to 91% in model forward passes without additional retraining. That figure describes the reported reduction in passes, while the broader contribution is a plug-and-play decoding framework that exploits spatial locality to improve generation efficiency.
icml-2025-zipar-parallel-autoregressive-.tldr: ZipAR uses spatial locality for parallel image-token decoding, reducing Emu3-Gen forward passes by up to 91% without retraining.
